analysis.one_liner: Caps Wall Street speculation in oil markets and sets a 12% margin requirement to lower gas prices.
analysis.headline: The bill to curb oil speculation never got a hearing or a vote; it sat in the House Agriculture Committee for the rest of the two-year Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have ordered the top commodity regulator, within 14 days of becoming law, to cap how many oil futures and swap contracts financial speculators can hold, require 12% down on speculative energy trades, and force banks and hedge funds trading energy for their own accounts to register as speculators. Its stated goal was to push crude oil and gasoline prices back toward what supply and demand fundamentals support. Airlines and companies hedging real business risks would have been exempt.
analysis.who_benefits: Drivers and businesses paying fuel prices. The bill's findings cite an average gas price of $3.75 a gallon in June 2011, an Exxon Mobil CEO statement that oil 'should cost between $60 and $70 per barrel' on fundamentals, and a Goldman Sachs warning to clients that speculators were adding as much as $27 a barrel to crude [S3]. If speculation was inflating prices as the findings argue, position caps and higher margin would take that pressure off the pump price. Airlines and other companies buying fuel to hedge real operations keep their exemption.

how_it_helps.text: Would have required the CFTC Chairman within 14 days of enactment to set speculative position limits on crude oil, gasoline, diesel, jet fuel, and heating oil futures and swaps, matching the limits of the New York Mercantile Exchange and applied across U.S. exchanges, foreign exchanges reachable from the U.S., and swap contracts [S2] [S3].
Would have set a 12% margin (down payment) requirement on speculative energy futures and swaps, making it costlier to gamble with borrowed leverage [S2] [S3].

Would have required bank holding companies, investment banks, hedge funds, and swap dealers trading energy futures for their own benefit, or for index funds and ETFs, to register as noncommercial speculators and count every position against the limits [S2] [S3].

Would have capped all noncommercial speculators at 35% of total positions in these markets, and exempted bona-fide hedging — airlines locking in jet fuel, refiners locking in crude — so real businesses could keep managing risk [S3].
Its authority would have ended once the CFTC itself imposed the position limits that the Dodd-Frank law already required, framing the bill as an emergency backstop against regulatory delay [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Wall Street banks, hedge funds, and swap dealers trading energy futures and swaps for profit. Position caps and a 12% margin requirement shrink the size of the bets they can make with leverage, and treating index-fund and ETF-linked positions as their own speculative positions limits a popular vehicle for betting on oil. Oil producers would also see less revenue if prices fell toward the $60-$70 per barrel level cited in the bill's findings.
analysis.who_pays_short: Big banks and hedge funds trading oil futures

drawbacks.text: The premise that speculators, not supply and demand, drove 2011 prices is contested; the bill leans on statements from an oil company CEO, a Goldman Sachs client note, and Saudi officials, but economists have long debated how much financial speculation moves oil prices versus physical supply, demand, and geopolitics [S3].

The bill directs the regulator's Chairman to act 'unilaterally' within 14 days, skipping the notice-and-comment process that normally lets affected firms and the public contest a rule — a shortcut that would likely have drawn legal challenge, as the CFTC's later, procedurally regular position-limits rule did.

A 12% margin is far above the exchange margins traders actually posted at the time; higher margin raises hedging costs for some market users and can pull liquidity out of the market, which could widen day-to-day price swings rather than narrow them.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: If the bill's premise was right, the payoff was broad: even a few dollars of speculative premium out of the price of a gallon of gas dwarfs any hedging-cost inconvenience for ordinary households. The risks are real but narrower — a contested diagnosis, a rushed rulemaking process, and margin high enough to tax legitimate risk management. The design (real-business hedgers exempt, sunset once Dodd-Frank limits take effect) is targeted rather than sweeping, which weighs in its favor.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on June 23, 2011, referred to the House Agriculture Committee, then sent to a subcommittee — and no hearing, markup, or vote ever followed before the Congress ended in January 2013 [S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Maurice Hinchey introduced the bill on June 23, 2011, joined by Reps. Welch, DeFazio, Grijalva, Olver, and Stark as original sponsors [S3].

The House referred it to the Agriculture Committee on the day of introduction — the committee with jurisdiction over commodity futures trading — and on July 13, 2011, referred it to its Subcommittee on General Farm Commodities and Risk Management [S5].
No further action was ever recorded; the bill died at the end of the 112th Congress on January 3, 2013 [S1] [S5].
All 13 cosponsors were House Democrats, and the bill received no hearing or roll call in the Republican-controlled chamber [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The banks, hedge funds, and swap dealers trading energy futures kept unlimited speculative positions and their existing low margin requirements. The CFTC's own Dodd-Frank position-limits rule remained tied up in rulemaking and litigation rather than the faster mandate this bill would have imposed.

industries.industry: Energy futures and swap traders (big banks, hedge funds, swap dealers)
industries.note: The bill caps their speculative positions at NYMEX levels, sets a 12% margin on speculative energy trades, and forces proprietary index-fund trading onto their position limits — directly shrinking their oil-trading business. Its gain (unlimited leveraged speculation) comes at the pump price ordinary drivers pay.

If the bill pushed prices toward the $60-$70 per barrel fundamentals cited in its own findings, producers would collect less per barrel. Their physical hedging was exempt, so the hit is on revenue, not risk management.

The bill's own findings quote Delta's general counsel on the marginal cost of production, and bona-fide hedgers are exempt — so these businesses would keep hedging freely while potentially paying less at the wholesale and retail level.
